strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-documented gap: Table 1 and Section 2 convincingly show that existing AFC benchmarks require external CFD solvers, lack uniform differentiability, and offer limited 3D/MARL support; FluidGym is the first suite combining all four desiderata in a single PyTorch stack.

Strong engineering and usability: pip-installable, Gymnasium/PettingZoo/SB3/TorchRL compatible, no external solver dependency, multi-GPU parallelization, and documented per-step runtimes (Table 2) that make the benchmark practically adoptable.

Careful evaluation methodology: standardized train/val/test splits with ten randomized initial domains, Agarwal et al. (2021) performance profiles with stratified bootstrap CIs, IQM reporting, and mean reward per step to avoid episode-length confounds — a level of rigor missing from much of the surveyed AFC literature.

Extensive experimental effort (over 16k GPU hours documented per environment in Table 7) plus transfer-learning studies (2D→3D cylinder, small→large TCF domain) that demonstrate the scientific utility of the suite beyond mere existence.

Environment validation against prior literature (cylinder drag vs. Rabault et al., RBC grid refinement study, airfoil vs. Wang et al., TCF opposition control vs. Guastoni et al.) provides confidence in simulation fidelity; solver was independently validated by Franz et al. (2026).
Fully differentiable step() demonstrated via D-MPC gradient-based control, showing reward gradients yield effective drag reduction, plus a formal treatment of differentiability in Appendix B.2.

Complete public release of environments, initial domains, trained models, and results; honest and thorough limitations section covering seed count, CUDA-only dependency, and off-the-shelf hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The 'MARL' support is weaker than the framing suggests: MA-PPO/MA-SAC are essentially independent agents sharing a translation-equivariant policy, with local/global reward mixing. No dedicated MARL methods (e.g., CTDE with centralized critics, QMIX/MAPPO variants) are evaluated, so desideratum (iii) is demonstrated architecturally rather than algorithmically.

Only 3-5 random seeds per environment, acknowledged in Section 5, limits the statistical power of the headline algorithmic conclusions (e.g., 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO'), particularly for the 3D airfoil/cylinder cases — and Figures 4 and 24-30 show overlapping confidence intervals in several comparisons.

The differentiability claim is under-explored: gradient correctness is never verified (e.g., against finite differences), the memory/time overhead of backpropagating through implicit PISO linear solves is not quantified, and D-MPC is demonstrated only on CylinderJet2D. Given that differentiability is the paper's second headline contribution, systematic characterization is warranted.

The 'comprehensive evaluation covering all FluidGym environments' claim (contribution 3) is overstated: Table 7 shows zero GPU hours (no experiments) for RBC wide variants, TCF bottom-wall variants, and Airfoil3D medium/hard, and Section 3.2 concedes only the easy 3D airfoil is run.

Baseline diversity is narrow: only PPO/SAC (and their multi-agent variants) with default SB3 hyperparameters. No benchmark comparisons against HydroGym or cross-platform result checks, and no gradient-based differentiable RL baselines despite motivating them heavily in the introduction.

Minor presentation issues: Table 7's GPU-hours formula (steps × seeds × seconds × algorithms) conflates wall-clock seconds with GPU-hours ambiguously; some environment/runtime details (e.g., why wide variants and TCF-bottom were excluded) appear only implicitly.
First-order implicit Euler time integration may limit accuracy for the harder (higher Re/Re_tau) regimes, and the validation is per-environment but limited to low-to-moderate settings for some cases.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a genuine gap: existing RL-for-AFC benchmarks rely on external CFD solvers, are rarely differentiable, and lack MARL/3D support; FluidGym's fully differentiable, single-Python-stack design built on the GPU-accelerated PICT solver directly targets these limitations, and the comparison table (Table 1) against prior benchmarks is fair and informative.

Substantial engineering effort and resource commitment are evident (reportedly >16k GPU hours), with released environments, datasets, trained models, and a standardized train/val/test protocol with deterministic seeding—this materially improves reproducibility in a field criticized for inconsistent evaluation.

The appendix provides meaningful physical validation of the environments (grid refinement for RBC, comparison of Cd/Cl/Nusselt numbers against prior literature), which is often missing in benchmark papers and lends credibility to the simulations.

The paper covers useful additional analyses: performance profiles in the style of Agarwal et al. (2021), IQM reporting, policy transfer from 2D to 3D and across domain sizes, and a gradient-based D-MPC baseline demonstrating the value of differentiability.
The limitations section is candid and honest about seed counts, default hyperparameters, GPU-only execution, and the proof-of-concept nature of the D-MPC evaluation.
weaknesses: There is a significant inconsistency between the claimed scope of the experiments and what was actually run: the paper claims 'an extensive experimental study covering all FluidGym environments', yet Table 7 shows 0 GPU hours (i.e., no experiments) for numerous environments including all RBC2D-wide, RBC3D-wide, TCFSmall3D-bottom, TCFLarge3D-bottom, and the medium/hard Airfoil3D variants. Many of the 13 advertised environments are defined but never evaluated, weakening the central contribution as presented.

The algorithmic evaluation is thin for a benchmark paper: only PPO and SAC (and their MA- variants) with default SB3 hyperparameters, evaluated on 5 seeds (3 for expensive 3D tasks). The headline finding that SAC outperforms PPO is already well established in the AFC literature, so the experimental insights offer limited new understanding beyond confirming prior results on new environments.

Statistical robustness is limited: with 3-5 seeds and the acknowledged high variance of RL, several conclusions (e.g., MA-SAC vs. MA-PPO differences 'within confidence intervals', transfer results that are 'on par, slightly below') are not strongly supported. Some reported results are puzzling and unexamined, e.g., PPO achieving negative drag reduction (-4.7%) on CylinderJet3D-hard while SAC fails (-0.5%), which warrants analysis rather than tabulation.

The differentiability claim, a key selling point, is only exercised via a minimal D-MPC proof of concept on a single 2D environment (CylinderJet2D). No comparison with other differentiable simulation approaches or gradient-based methods (e.g., DPC, differentiable RL) is provided, so the practical benefit of end-to-end differentiability remains largely undemonstrated.

The 'first standalone, fully differentiable' claim is somewhat overstated given HydroGym's partial JAX-based differentiability and the existence of general PDE-control benchmarks; the positioning relies on a specific conjunction of desiderata.

Dependencies on components that are themselves unpublished or future-dated (the PICT solver, cited as Franz et al., 2026) complicate reproducibility of the underlying simulation stack, and CUDA-only execution restricts accessibility.

The scope is specialized: for the ICML audience, the contribution is primarily an engineering/platform effort with limited methodological novelty; the learning-science insights are modest (confirming SAC > PPO, plausible MARL coordination observations), so the paper's significance hinges almost entirely on community adoption of the benchmark, which is not yet evidenced.

strengths: FluidGym fills a genuine gap: Table 1 convincingly shows no prior RL-for-AFC benchmark simultaneously offers standalone Python installation, full differentiability, MARL support, and 3D environments. The combination of these desiderata (Section 3.1) is well motivated by concrete limitations of existing tools.

Substantial experimental effort (~16k GPU hours, Table 7) covering PPO, SAC, MA-PPO, MA-SAC, and a gradient-based D-MPC baseline across four environment classes with three difficulty levels, including useful transfer studies (2D->3D and small->large domain) that showcase benchmark capabilities beyond simple training curves.

Methodologically sound evaluation practices for a benchmark paper: rliable performance profiles with stratified bootstrap CIs (Figure 4), IQM test metrics, a train/val/test split protocol with standardized initial domains, and per-environment quantitative test tables (Tables 8-11) rather than only training rewards.

Honest and thorough limitations section: low seed counts, CUDA-only solver, default hyperparameters, and incomplete coverage of gradient-based methods are all transparently acknowledged rather than hidden.

Good reproducibility posture: environments, trained models, datasets, and hyperparameter configurations (Tables 5-6) are publicly released; the interface is compatible with Gymnasium/PettingZoo/SB3/TorchRL, lowering adoption barriers.

Numerical validation of the underlying PICT solver in Appendix B (grid refinement for RBC, comparison of cylinder drag, airfoil coefficients, and TCF opposition-control results against prior literature) strengthens trust in the simulation fidelity.
weaknesses: Coverage of the claimed benchmark is incomplete: several advertised environments receive zero GPU hours in Table 7 (RBC2D-wide, RBC3D-wide, Airfoil3D medium/hard, all TCF bottom variants), and the medium/hard Airfoil3D cases are explicitly excluded. The paper thus introduces 13 environments but validates baselines on a substantial subset, which weakens the claim of a fully populated benchmark.

Statistical robustness is limited: only 3-5 seeds, and the authors themselves concede that algorithmic comparisons (a central selling point) are underpowered. Some results are ambiguous, e.g., CylinderJet3D-hard shows near-zero or negative drag reduction for PPO/SAC (Table 8), which deserves deeper analysis than it receives.

Originality is moderate: the contribution is primarily an integration effort around the PICT solver (Franz et al., 2026, a companion/independent work), and several environments closely follow prior setups (Rabault et al. 2019; Vignon et al. 2023; Vasanth et al. 2024). The novelty is in packaging and scope rather than new methods or new physical insight.

Dependence on PICT introduces a single point of failure and a somewhat circular validation story (solver validated by its own companion paper; TCF validation deemed unnecessary for that reason). Cross-validation against established solvers (OpenFOAM, FEniCS) would be more convincing, especially given the 3.84% deviation in cylinder drag.

The hyperparameter treatment (default SB3 settings for everything) is defensible for comparability but the paper's conclusions about SAC vs. PPO and MARL benefits are drawn from a single, untuned configuration per algorithm; this limits the strength of the empirical findings.

Presentation issues: the release URL is missing in the abstract and the introduction (sentences end with 'available at' with no link), which is problematic for a paper whose central contribution is a released resource. Additionally, some physical validation details (e.g., justification that Re=100/250/500 map to appropriate turbulence levels in 3D) are only asserted, not shown.
No direct empirical comparison against any existing benchmark (e.g., running the same algorithm in HydroGym), so the claimed advantages remain architectural (Table 1) rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Fills a genuine and clearly articulated gap: existing AFC benchmarks (DRLinFluids, drlFoam, Gym-preCICE, Beacon, HydroGym) rely on external CFD solvers, lack differentiability, and offer little 3D/MARL support; FluidGym's Table 1 comparison substantiates the claimed differentiation.

Substantial experimental investment (~27k GPU hours per Table 8) with a rigorous evaluation methodology aligned with modern RL benchmarking practice (Agarwal et al. performance profiles, IQM, stratified bootstrap 95% CIs, per-step normalized metrics), directly addressing the reproducibility deficiencies the authors document in the literature.

Numerical validation of the underlying PICT-based environments against prior work for all four flow classes (cylinder vs. Rabault et al., RBC grid refinement study, airfoil vs. Wang et al., TCF opposition control at 20% consistent with Guastoni et al.), which strengthens the credibility of the benchmark's physics.

Useful and non-obvious empirical findings: DPC achieving order-of-magnitude speedups via reward gradients on 2D tasks, robust 2D-to-3D policy transfer for the cylinder, and small-domain-to-large-domain transfer outperforming direct large-domain training for TCF, demonstrating the suite's scientific value beyond infrastructure alone.

Comprehensive supporting material: full environment definitions, difficulty parameterization, hyperparameter tables for all algorithms, hardware specs, runtime accounting, qualitative flow-field visualizations, and a PPO network-size ablation; release of environments, datasets, and trained models supports reproducibility.
Honest, specific limitations section (seed count, CUDA-only execution, restricted DPC coverage, off-the-shelf hyperparameters) that is candid rather than dismissive.
weaknesses: Evaluation coverage is incomplete relative to the claimed suite: several advertised environment variants (RBC2D-WIDE, RBC3D-WIDE, all -BOTTOM TCF variants) were never run (0 GPU hours in Table 8), and medium/hard Airfoil3D cases were excluded for computational reasons, so benchmark conclusions rest on a subset of the 13 environments.

Statistical robustness is thin for the most informative comparisons: five seeds (four for MA-PPO on Airfoil3D-hard) with overlapping confidence intervals, as the authors themselves concede; several headline claims (e.g., 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO', 'MA-SAC exhibits marginally higher scores') rest on differences partially within CIs.

Baseline performance on the hardest tasks is weak or near-zero (e.g., CylinderJet3D-hard drag reductions of 0.9-2.4%, MA-SAC negative on CylinderJet3D-hard, MA-PPO ~0.1% on TCF-hard), leaving it unclear whether these difficulty levels are well-posed control tasks or whether default hyperparameters simply fail; this limits the benchmark's immediate utility for the 'hard' tiers.

Differentiability is a headline contribution, yet gradient-based evaluation is limited to DPC on two 2D environments, and DPC training degraded and was stopped early on one of them; no differentiable-RL baselines are included, so the differentiability claim is demonstrated only narrowly.

The 'first' and 'high-fidelity' framing is somewhat strong: grids and resolutions are modest for turbulent regimes (e.g., 128×65×128 for TCF at Re_tau up to 550 with first-order implicit Euler time stepping), and validation against single prior studies with acknowledged deviations (3.84% cylinder drag, 2.3% Nu) rather than rigorous convergence evidence for all cases.

Default SB3 hyperparameters applied uniformly (acknowledged in the paper) may confound algorithmic conclusions; the PPO network ablation covers only two environments and does not extend to SAC or other sensitive settings (e.g., TCF gradient-step reduction for SAC).

Minor presentation issues: some formatting inconsistencies in tables (e.g., '620' in Table 8, 'TAact' vs 'Tact' in Appendix C), and the URL/software links are blank in the provided manuscript, making the 'available at' reproducibility claim unverifiable within the text.

strengths: Genuinely addresses a documented gap: the paper motivates the need well (Table 1 comparison, Section 2 discussion of inconsistent evaluation practices in AFC literature) and the resulting artifact is the first benchmark combining standalone PyTorch execution, end-to-end differentiability, MARL support, and 3D environments.

The experimental scale is substantial and transparent: ~27k GPU hours are tabulated per-environment (Table 8), five random seeds with ten test episodes are used consistently, and the analysis follows established best practice (Agarwal et al. performance profiles with bootstrap CIs, IQM aggregation), which is more rigorous than much of the prior AFC literature the paper criticizes.
Good release discipline: environments, initial domains, trained models, and full hyperparameter tables (Tables 5-7) plus hardware/software configurations (Appendix D) support reproducibility.

The environment validation effort is non-trivial: grid refinement for RBC (Table 3), comparisons against prior reported values for cylinder, airfoil, and TCF, and an opposition-control and PD-controller baseline give the physics side credibility.
The transfer studies (2D→3D, small→large TCF domain) and the emerging coordinated MARL behavior in RBC3D are interesting, useful demonstrations beyond pure infrastructure.
Honest limitations section: the authors explicitly acknowledge seed limitations, CUDA-only execution, default hyperparameters, and the restricted scope of DPC experiments rather than overselling.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The core solver (PICT, Franz et al. 2026) is prior work; the contribution is integration, environment definition, and benchmarking. This is a legitimate but primarily engineering/artifact contribution, and the paper does not demonstrate any fundamentally new insight about learning in flow control.

The evidence for the central selling point — that full differentiability unlocks better control learning — is thin. DPC is evaluated on only two 2D environments, its training degrades on CylinderJet2D-easy (Figure 5 note), and it is not shown to ultimately outperform standard RL on test metrics (e.g., CylinderJet2D-easy: DPC 4.335% vs. SAC 6.697% drag reduction in Table 9). The claim that this 'underscores the value of FluidGym as the first fully differentiable AFC benchmark' is not yet strongly supported at scale.

Baseline conclusions may be unfair: default SB3 hyperparameters with PPO network sizes of [64,64] versus SAC's [256,256] (Tables 5-6) make cross-algorithm comparisons (e.g., 'SAC reliably outperforms PPO') questionable as statements about algorithms rather than configurations. The network-size ablation (Appendix E.5) covers only two environments.

Coverage inconsistencies: several environments defined in the benchmark were never evaluated (all -wide RBC variants, all -bottom TCF variants, Airfoil3D medium/hard) — Table 8 lists zero GPU hours for them — so the 'diverse, complete' framing overstates what the study actually delivers, and results for missing cases (e.g., Airfoil3D-hard with only MA-PPO, four seeds) are incomplete.

Runtime is a practical concern that limits adoption: 28-53 s/step on an A100 for the airfoil environments (Table 2) means the 'plug-and-play' accessibility claim is undermined by expensive hard tasks; feasibility for the target community of non-CFD experts should be discussed more concretely.

Statistical robustness remains limited (five seeds, occasionally four), and several reported gaps (e.g., Figure 4, MA-PPO vs. MA-SAC) are acknowledged to fall within confidence intervals, weakening the headline algorithmic findings.

Reproducibility of the specific numbers relies on custom CUDA kernels and pre-built wheels; without CPU-only execution or broader hardware validation, independent verification of the full suite is non-trivial.

strengths: FluidGym addresses a genuine and clearly documented gap: existing AFC benchmarks either depend on external CFD solvers, lack differentiability, or offer limited 3D/MARL support (Table 1 comparison is fair and well-researched). A standalone, fully differentiable PyTorch suite is a useful contribution to the RL-for-flow-control community.

The experimental study is substantial (over 25k GPU hours, Table 8), covers four flow classes across 2D/3D and difficulty levels, and uses evaluation methodology (IQM, performance profiles after Agarwal et al. 2021, stratified bootstrap CIs, per-step metrics) that is notably more rigorous than typical practice in this literature.

The paper demonstrates real use of the differentiability claim: DPC baseline experiments (Section 4.3) show ~1-2 orders of magnitude sample-efficiency gains over PPO/SAC, giving concrete evidence the benchmark enables gradient-based control research, not just classical RL.

Solver and environment validation against prior literature (cylinder drag within 3.84% of Rabault et al., RBC grid refinement study, airfoil lift/drag vs. Wang et al., TCF opposition control at ~20% drag reduction consistent with Guastoni et al.) supports physical correctness.
Excellent reproducibility posture: released environments, datasets, trained models, unified train/val/test splits with seeded RNG, full hyperparameter tables (Appendix D), and runtime benchmarks.

The transfer-learning studies (2D->3D, small->large TCF domain) are a genuinely interesting experimental component enabled by the benchmark's design and yield a non-obvious finding (small-domain MARL policies transfer well and outperform large-domain-trained policies).
Honest limitations section: authors acknowledge limited seeds, CUDA-only requirement, DPC restricted to 2D environments, and default hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Scientific novelty is primarily engineering and integration rather than new understanding; environment designs largely follow prior work (Vignon et al. 2023, Vasanth et al. 2024, Rabault et al. 2019, Suarez et al. 2025), and the core algorithmic findings (SAC competitive with or better than PPO) are modest and partly within confidence intervals, as the authors themselves note.

Only five random seeds are used, which the authors acknowledge limits statistical robustness of the central algorithmic comparisons; several headline conclusions (e.g., MA-SAC marginally higher than MA-PPO) rest on differences the paper admits lie within confidence intervals.

The claimed contribution of 'covering all core FluidGym environment classes and difficulty levels' is inconsistent with Table 8: all RBC2D-WIDE, RBC3D-WIDE, and *-BOTTOM variants show 0 GPU hours because they were 'not evaluated separately.' This coverage gap should be stated more prominently.

The min-max normalized scores used in the aggregate analysis (Figure 4) are normalized independently per environment-difficulty pair against the best-performing run, introducing a mild circularity: the top-performing algorithm partially defines the scale on which all algorithms are ranked.

Baseline evaluation uses default SB3 hyperparameters for comparability, but this handicaps conclusions about 'algorithmic performance'; the ablation addressing this covers only PPO network size on two environments, which is thin given the paper's claims about SAC vs. PPO.
The PPO device is set to CPU (Table 5) while SAC uses CUDA; this is unexplained and potentially confounds the runtime comparisons in Figure 9 and per-step runtime claims.

Gradient-based (DPC) evaluation is limited to two 2D environments, with training even degrading and stopping early on CylinderJet2D-easy; the claim that FluidGym establishes 'a scalable foundation for gradient-based learning' is therefore only weakly evidenced in 3D settings.

Incomplete coverage in key tables: 3D airfoil medium/hard results are missing for several algorithms, and one case uses four instead of five seeds, making the aggregate profiles uneven across environments.
